clue.text: Drunk pinching sailor's footwear

indicators.note: to pinch is to nip something between finger and thumb, so the word for a drunk closes round the sailor

parts.note: a sot is a habitual drunkard, so drunk is a noun here, not an adjective
AB is the abbreviation for able-bodied seaman, a rank of sailor

explanation.surface: A drunkard is caught stealing a sailor's shoes.
explanation.walkthrough: 'pinching' means stealing in the surface, but here it means gripping: the drunk holds the sailor inside. 'Drunk' is a noun, the person, not a description of anyone.
explanation.definitionFit: A sabot is a wooden clog once worn by French and Belgian peasants, so it is an example of something worn on the foot.

clue.text: Economies reversed: school's given decoration

indicators.note: reversed tells you to write the word for economies from its last letter back to its first

parts.note: economies are savings made by spending less, which are cuts
a coed is a school that teaches boys and girls together, short for coeducational

explanation.surface: With the budget cuts overturned, a school finally gets a fresh coat of paint.
explanation.walkthrough: 'reversed' turns CUTS into STUC. In the surface the economies are a policy being overturned so that the school can be done up; 'school's' supplies a noun, a mixed school.
explanation.definitionFit: Stucco is fine plaster used for ornamental mouldings, so a wall or ceiling finished with it has had ornament applied, a synonym in the past participle.

clue.text: Girl outside reporting to base gets it wrong

indicators.note: outside says the word for a girl goes round the other two pieces, with part of it on each flank

parts.note: a miss is a girl or young unmarried woman
an employee reporting to a manager works under that manager
a base is a support that something rests on, such as a stand for a lamp or a vase

explanation.surface: A young woman out in the field radios headquarters and makes a mistake.
explanation.walkthrough: 'outside' wraps the girl round the other two pieces. The surface suggests a soldier radioing headquarters; in fact 'reporting to' is about rank at work and 'base' is a support for an object.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone who misunderstands fails to grasp what was meant, a synonym for making an error of interpretation, with the same third-person verb ending.

clue.text: Pleasure to replace part in special mode of transport

indicators.note: to replace says the word for pleasure takes over the spot held by the letters of part

parts.note: particular means special, as in taking particular care over something
the letters of part stand as written at the front of the longer word and are the ones swapped out
fun is pleasure or enjoyment

explanation.surface: A mechanic is glad to fit a new component in an unusual vehicle.
explanation.walkthrough: 'to replace' swaps the PART at the front of PARTICULAR for FUN. 'special mode of transport' reads as one phrase, but 'special' belongs to the wordplay and only the last three words define.
explanation.definitionFit: A funicular is a cable-hauled railway that climbs a steep hillside, so it is an example of a way of getting about.

clue.text: Beat that heralds rock or blues first of all

indicators.note: first of all asks for the opening letter of every one of the five words that stand between it and the definition

explanation.surface: A drum rhythm announces the start of a rock or blues number.
explanation.walkthrough: 'first of all' sounds like 'to begin with', but it asks for the initial letter of all five words between 'Beat' and itself.
explanation.definitionFit: To throb is to pulse with a strong regular rhythm, as a heart or a bass line does, a synonym as verb or as noun.

clue.text: Something eaten with pained expression in appearance? On the contrary

parts.note: nosh is British slang for food, a word borrowed from Yiddish
ow is what you cry out when something hurts

explanation.surface: A dish looks as if it was eaten with a grimace, but the diner insists otherwise.
explanation.walkthrough: 'On the contrary' often tells you to swap two pieces round, with 'in' as the container; here it is part of the definition, the opposite of an appearance. The 'expression' is a cry, not a look on the face.
explanation.definitionFit: A no-show is someone who fails to turn up when expected, which is the opposite of putting in an appearance.

clue.text: Rule concerning northern church writer

parts.note: a law is a rule that everyone must obey
re means about or concerning, as at the head of a business letter
N is the standard abbreviation for north or northern
CE is the abbreviation for the Church of England

explanation.surface: A regulation is laid down about an author attached to a church in the north.
explanation.walkthrough: Four pieces follow one another with no indicator. The writer is DH Lawrence, the English novelist of Sons and Lovers; CE is the Church of England, the country's established church.
explanation.definitionFit: DH Lawrence, the English novelist who wrote Sons and Lovers, is one famous example of an author.

clue.text: Has desire, burning — it's unlikely to succeed

definitions.note: the answer is a noun but the definition is a whole clause: it stands for the thing being defined, which is described instead of named

parts.note: someone who has desire for a thing longs for it
something burning is very hot, like a burning forehead

explanation.surface: Someone is consumed by a passion that has little chance of being fulfilled.
explanation.walkthrough: 'burning' seems to describe the desire but is a piece of its own. The join between the two pieces falls one letter after the gap between the answer's two words.
explanation.definitionFit: A long shot is a bet or attempt with only a slim chance of coming off, so the clause describes it instead of naming it.

clue.text: Logical bloke backing firm

indicators.note: backing here means standing behind, so the bloke is written after the firm, like a backer at its rear

parts.note: a firm is a company, shortened to Co in business names
bloke is British slang for a man, and gent is short for gentleman

explanation.surface: A clear-thinking man puts his money behind a company.
explanation.walkthrough: 'backing' often turns a word round, but here it only places the bloke behind the firm, as a backer stands behind a venture. Bloke is British slang for a man.
explanation.definitionFit: A cogent argument is clear, well reasoned and convincing, so the adjective is a near-synonym for sound in its reasoning.

clue.text: Rock fish found by son

indicators.note: found by means discovered next to, so the fish is set beside the son, who comes first

parts.note: S is the abbreviation for son in family trees
a hake is a sea fish of the cod family, widely eaten in Britain and Spain

explanation.surface: A boy comes across a fish that lives among the rocks.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rock fish' reads as one creature, but the words part company: 'Rock' is a verb meaning to sway, and only 'fish' is the animal. 'found by' sets the fish beside the son.
explanation.definitionFit: To rock something is to move it to and fro, and shaking it does the same more violently, so the verbs are near-synonyms.

clue.text: Flight from prison clutching a holdall?

indicators.note: clutching means gripping tightly, so the word for prison closes round the single letter that follows it in the clue

parts.note: stir is slang for prison, as in the phrase stir crazy
taken as written
a holdall is a large soft travel bag, one example of a case; the question mark admits it is only an example

explanation.surface: An escaped convict runs from jail gripping a travel bag.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Flight' looks like an escape but is a run of steps between floors. 'clutching' has the prison grip the A, and the question mark admits a holdall is only one example of a case.
explanation.definitionFit: A flight is an unbroken run of stairs between two floors or landings, so the two nouns are synonyms.

clue.text: Picture hat (garish) dandy fashioned

indicators.note: fashioned means made or shaped, so the letters of the three words before it are worked into a new form

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written; the brackets are only punctuation
taken as written

explanation.surface: A fop designed a gaudy wide-brimmed hat.
explanation.walkthrough: 'fashioned' rearranges HAT, GARISH and DANDY together. A picture hat is a woman's wide-brimmed hat, but 'Picture' breaks away to mean a film: the Beatles' first, from 1964.
explanation.definitionFit: A Hard Day's Night is the Beatles' 1964 musical comedy, and picture is an older word for a cinema film.

clue.text: Article about Republican surrounded by gun society members

indicators.note: surrounded by says everything built so far sits inside the word for a gun, which closes in on both flanks

parts.note: the Bren is a light machine gun used by the British Army from the 1930s

indicators.note: about means around, so the article is wrapped round the letter for Republican

parts.note: the is the definite article in grammar
R is the abbreviation for Republican in American politics

explanation.surface: A news story covers a Republican politician hemmed in by members of a gun club.
explanation.walkthrough: 'about' wraps THE round R, and 'surrounded by' puts that inside the gun. 'gun society' reads as a shooting club, but 'gun' is wordplay: a Bren is a British Army machine gun.
explanation.definitionFit: Brethren is an old plural of brother, now used for the fellow members of a religious order, guild or lodge.

clue.text: Ale with no head that's weird

indicators.note: the head of a word is its first letter, so with no head means the word for ale loses its opening letter

parts.note: ale is a type of beer
that's is short for that is, which is written ie, from the Latin id est

explanation.surface: A pint pulled without any froth on top strikes the drinker as odd.
explanation.walkthrough: 'with no head' takes the B off BEER, leaving EER. 'that's' looks like a mere link, but read in full as 'that is' it gives IE.
explanation.definitionFit: Something eerie is strange in an unsettling, ghostly way, which makes it a close synonym of uncanny.

clue.text: One of four maybe succeeded as film tie-in arranged

parts.note: S is the abbreviation for succeeded, as used in lists of monarchs and family trees

indicators.note: arranged means put into order, so the letters of the three words before it are set out afresh

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written
taken as written, ignoring the hyphen

explanation.surface: One product in a range of four did well once it was packaged as a movie spin-off.
explanation.walkthrough: 'arranged' reorders the three words before it, behind the letter that 'succeeded' abbreviates to. Four is the usual number left in the round before a final, though not the only one, so the definition ends with a qualifier.
explanation.definitionFit: A knockout tournament's penultimate round normally has four players or teams left, and each of them answers this description.

clue.text: Seaman upset former pupil with shiner?

indicators.note: upset means overturned, and in a down answer that flips the two letters for the former pupil so they read upwards

parts.note: OB stands for old boy, the British term for a former pupil of a school
the sun is something that shines; the question mark flags this playful description

explanation.surface: A sailor distressed an old schoolmate by giving him a black eye.
explanation.walkthrough: 'upset' turns OB over to give BO. A shiner is slang for a black eye, which is how the surface reads; the question mark admits it simply means a thing that shines.
explanation.definitionFit: A bosun, short for boatswain, is the ship's officer in charge of the deck crew and rigging, so he is one type of sailor.

clue.text: Persistent getting up final account — promises to pay

indicators.note: getting up means rising, and in a down answer a rising word is read from its bottom letter to its top

parts.note: net means final, what is left after all deductions, as in the net result
AC is a bookkeeping abbreviation for account, often written a/c
IOUs are signed notes saying I owe you, each one a promise to pay a debt

explanation.surface: A dogged bookkeeper draws up the last bill and collects pledges that it will be settled.
explanation.walkthrough: 'getting up' reads as drawing up the final account, but it only lifts NET, which becomes TEN in this down answer. The dash is just punctuation.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone tenacious keeps a firm grip and refuses to give up, which is the sense of the adjective dogged.

clue.text: Proper tips from sensible exam lady

indicators.note: the tips of a word are its two extremities, so take the first and last letters from each of the three words that follow

explanation.surface: A level-headed woman who runs the exams hands out sound advice.
explanation.walkthrough: 'tips from' takes the first and last letters of each of the three words after it. In the surface the tips are pieces of advice, with 'Proper' describing them.
explanation.definitionFit: Seemly behaviour is decent and in keeping with good manners, so the adjective is a synonym for decorous or correct.

clue.text: Puts recycled paper, not going with current

indicators.note: recycled material is broken down and made into something new, so the four letters of the word before it are remade in another order

parts.note: taken as written
a ream is a quantity of paper, once 480 sheets and now 500

explanation.surface: An office stocks recycled paper, refusing to follow the latest fashion.
explanation.walkthrough: 'recycled' turns PUTS into UPST; 'recycled paper' reads as one thing, but only 'paper' gives the ream. The current is a river's, so the definition means against the flow.
explanation.definitionFit: Travelling upstream means heading towards a river's source, against the flow of the water, so the phrase describes that direction.

clue.text: Talk about new melody

indicators.note: about means around, so the word for talk goes round the letter for new

parts.note: to chat is to talk in a friendly, informal way
N is the abbreviation for new, as in NT for New Testament

explanation.surface: People are discussing a tune that has just come out.
explanation.walkthrough: 'about' reads as 'on the subject of' but means around: the talk wraps the N. In church music a chant is a short tune to which psalms are sung, hence 'melody'.
explanation.definitionFit: In church music a chant is the short repeated tune to which psalms are sung, so it is one type of tune.

clue.text: In from Paris, pure at heart, in fling maybe that's potential to last

parts.note: en is the French word for in, and from Paris tells you to translate it into French

indicators.note: this second in says the heart of pure is placed inside the word for a fling

parts.note: the Highland fling is a lively Scottish dance; the second word marks it as only one example

indicators.note: the heart of a word is its centre, so take the two middle letters of the four-letter word before it

explanation.surface: Someone just back from Paris, innocent at heart, wonders whether a brief romance could endure.
explanation.walkthrough: 'from Paris' turns In into French, 'at heart' picks UR from pure, and the second 'in' drops it into the dance. The surface's fling is a brief romance; the wordplay's is the Highland fling, a Scottish dance.
explanation.definitionFit: Stamina, the staying power that lets a person or thing keep going for a long time, is a synonym.

clue.text: Baby teeth are treated in play centre

indicators.note: treated means given treatment, as a dentist treats teeth, so the letters of the three words before it are worked into a new order

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A dentist looks after toddlers' milk teeth at a children's soft-play centre.
explanation.walkthrough: 'treated' rearranges BABY TEETH ARE. A play centre sounds like somewhere for toddlers, but these plays are stage dramas: the Abbey is Ireland's national theatre, in Dublin.
explanation.definitionFit: The Abbey in Dublin is Ireland's national playhouse, a venue where stage dramas are put on, so the phrase is a punning description of it.

clue.text: One heat burns if careless?

indicators.note: careless work is slapdash and untidy, so the letters of the two words in the middle of the clue are thrown into a different order

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: Heat will scorch a person who does not take care.
explanation.walkthrough: 'careless' rearranges HEAT BURNS, and the whole clue doubles as the definition: a person whom heat burns if they take no care. 'One' and 'if' serve only that reading.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone lying out to get a tan ends up with scorched skin when they neglect the lotion, so the whole sentence describes that person.

clue.text: River trip captivates initially obdurate relative

indicators.note: to captivate is literally to take captive, so the word for a trip holds the other two pieces prisoner inside it

parts.note: a ride is a short trip in or on a vehicle

indicators.note: initially asks for just the first letter of the word that follows it

parts.note: gran is the informal British word for a grandmother

explanation.surface: A boat outing on the river wins over a family member who was stubborn at first.
explanation.walkthrough: 'captivates' means charms in the surface but takes captive here, holding the letter 'initially' picks and the relative. 'River trip' splits, leaving 'River' to define the one on the US-Mexico border.
explanation.definitionFit: The Rio Grande flows from Colorado to the Gulf of Mexico and forms the border between Texas and Mexico, so it is an example.

clue.text: Have regard for Councillor welcoming working party

indicators.note: to welcome guests is to take them in, so the abbreviation for the councillor takes the next two pieces inside it

parts.note: Cr is an abbreviation for Councillor, as printed before a name in local council papers
a machine that is working is on, as opposed to off
a party to a dispute or a contract is one side in it

explanation.surface: Spare a thought for the local councillor who has to greet a committee of inquiry.
explanation.walkthrough: 'welcoming' has CR take in ON and SIDE. A working party is a committee set up to study one problem, which is how the surface reads; here the two words are separate pieces.
explanation.definitionFit: To consider other people is to take their needs into account when acting, a synonym for the verb phrase in the clue.

clue.text: Defile that vessel first

indicators.note: first says the vessel, though named second in the clue, is written ahead of the word for that

parts.note: a can is a metal vessel for liquids, such as a watering can or an oil can
yon is an old or dialect word for that, as in yon hill

explanation.surface: Someone is told to desecrate that sacred cup before any other.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Defile' reads as a verb, to pollute, but as a noun it is a narrow pass between hills. 'first' moves the vessel to the front, ahead of YON, an old word for 'that'.
explanation.definitionFit: A defile is a narrow pass or gorge between steep hills, and a canyon is a deep one, so the nouns are near-synonyms.

clue.text: Flier feels upset about ignoring outsiders

indicators.note: the outsiders of a word are its first and last letters, and ignoring them leaves only what lies between

parts.note: someone who feels upset about a thing they did regrets it

explanation.surface: A pilot is distressed at having snubbed people from outside the group.
explanation.walkthrough: 'ignoring outsiders' strips the first and last letters, R and S, from REGRETS. 'upset' and 'about' each look like an instruction, but all three words 'feels upset about' simply mean regrets; the flier is a bird.
explanation.definitionFit: An egret is a white heron with long plumes, an example of a bird, and any bird is a creature that flies.

clue.text: Strange reply displays annoyance

indicators.note: displays says the answer is a run of letters hidden inside the words before it

parts.note: the letters run across the end of one word into the next

explanation.surface: An odd answer shows that the person is irritated.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Strange' tempts you to rearrange the five letters of 'reply', but nothing meaning annoyance comes out. 'displays' is the real indicator: the answer is on show across the two words before it, not after it.
explanation.definitionFit: Anger is a strong feeling of displeasure, and annoyance is a milder form of the same emotion, so the nouns are near-synonyms.
